cards.title: Prevent Clickjacking with Frame-Ancestors Header
cards.summary: Use the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive (or legacy X-Frame-Options) to stop competitors and attackers embedding your storefront in a frame and overlaying invisible buttons.
cards.use_when: Hardening your storefront or admin dashboard against clickjacking, e.g. when a third party could overlay a hidden add-to-cart or account action over an enticing button.
steps: Understand the attack: if your site allows framing, an attacker page can embed your site in a full-page iframe and transform/zoom it so a click lands on your real button (e.g. a social like button or an authenticated account action) while the user thinks they clicked something else.

Serverside, send the frame-ancestors directive in the response: 'none' to forbid all framing, or "'self'" to allow only your own origin to frame you. This is the reliable defense the source recommends over JS frame-busting.
Set the policy on every page or at the site-wide header level; do not assume you can detect at request time that a request is a framing attempt, since the server often cannot see it.
Verify on your own staging site by embedding your page in a test iframe and confirming the browser refuses to load it.
If you must support very old browsers, note the source says this header is long-supported and pervasive, but for other defensive headers check current browser support before relying on them.
caveats: Legacy X-Frame-Options with ALLOW-FROM is inconsistently supported; prefer frame-ancestors.
Frame-busting JavaScript is not a reliable defense per the cited Stanford research on busting frame busting.
Recently, browsers correctly require the entire embed chain to be same-origin; older behavior allowed an A->B->A chain. Verify with current browser behavior before relying on edge cases.

cards.title: Reject Cross-Site Form Submissions Using Origin Header
cards.summary: Check the Origin header against an allow list to block form POSTs from other sites; this does not stop request forgery but prevents the request from being accepted.
cards.use_when: Protecting storefront or checkout endpoints that accept form POSTs, such as changing an account email, applying a promo code, or placing an order, from being forged by a third-party page.
steps: Recognize that SameSite cookies only strip cookies from cross-site requests; they do not prevent the form submission itself, so the POST still arrives.
Serverside, read the Origin header on incoming POST requests and compare it against an allow list of origins you expect (e.g. your own storefront domain).
Reject requests whose Origin is missing or not on the allow list.

Note that GET requests are treated as CORS-simple and may not carry an Origin header for image/script/style loads; rely on the POST check for state-changing actions rather than expecting Origin everywhere.
Do not rely on the Referer header as a primary control; the source says it can be manipulated and is not reliable.
caveats: The browser sets and protects the Origin header; a site making the request cannot forge it, which is why it is trustworthy for this check.
You cannot truly stop a determined client (e.g. a script) from sending a request; the goal is to make your server reject requests it did not originate.

cards.title: Use Unpredictable URLs to Protect Private Media from Hotlinking
cards.summary: Stop bandwidth theft and leaked private assets by serving them from unguessable URLs instead of relying on Referer checks.
cards.use_when: Serving images such as user avatars, customer-uploaded photos, downloadable receipts, or paid content where hotlinking or leaking would cost bandwidth or expose private data.
steps: Identify assets where another site could embed the URL directly, causing you to pay for their traffic (hotlinking) or exposing logged-in-only content (e.g. an avatar that only appears when logged in).
Instead of exposing a predictable path, serve the asset from a URL that is difficult to guess (long random token) so only someone who knows the URL can load it.

Recognize that SameSite cookies will strip the login cookie on a third-party page, so an authenticated-only avatar will resolve to the logged-out image there, but this does not prevent the request itself.
Do not rely solely on the Referer header to block hotlinking; the source calls this not foolproof because the attacker can manipulate it.
caveats: An unguessable URL is a secrecy control, not authentication; anyone the URL is shared with can still use it.
This does not prevent the request from being made, only makes it unprofitable or unlinking to guess.

cards.title: Choose the Right Tool for Each Cross-Site Boundary Question
cards.summary: A decision framework mapping the same-origin questions (can A link to B, embed B, read B's data, submit forms, steal images/scripts) to reliable vs unreliable defenses.
cards.use_when: Architecting storefront integrations, embedded widgets, third-party scripts, or any cross-origin data sharing and needing to know which control actually holds.
steps: Can site A link to or embed site B? By default yes; block it with the frame-ancestors header if you don't want to be embedded, and the source says this works reliably.
Can site A embed B and modify B's DOM? No; the same-origin policy is strong here and there is no way to relax it, so this stays a safe default.
Can a site submit a form to you? You can reject cross-origin submissions by checking the Origin header, which the source says works quite reliably.
Do you want forms allowed but without cookies attached? Use SameSite cookies for that middle ground.
Can another site read the bytes of your response? No; strengthening this is not foolproof, and the source treats 'images and scripts' defenses as best-effort only.
When you need to intentionally allow cross-origin reads (e.g. collaborating with a partner API), plan to relax the policy explicitly rather than weakening defaults.
caveats: Only the frame-ancestors and Origin-allow-list controls are described as reliable; Referer-based and similar tricks are explicitly not foolproof.
Verify current browser behavior for any relaxation mechanism before shipping, since these details change.

cards.title: Kill Cross-Site Scripting by Escaping User Data at Output
cards.summary: Treat all user-supplied strings as data by HTML-escaping them before inserting them into your page, and consider the limits of blacklists.
cards.use_when: Building any storefront page that reflects user input, such as a search results page, a personalized welcome based on a URL parameter, or a product review display.
steps: Identify the pattern that causes the bug: server code concatenating a hard-coded HTML template with untrusted user input, so the browser cannot tell the user's string from your markup.

Understand the impact: an attacker who gets their text parsed as code can run script in your origin's context, taking actions as your logged-in customer (e.g. reading document.cookie and exfiltrating it, or submitting requests).
Fix it by escaping the untrusted value so angle brackets and other significant characters become inert HTML entities (e.g. < becomes <), so the browser displays the text instead of executing it.
Escape only the specific values that are user-supplied, not the entire page; escaping everything would turn your own tags into visible text.
Prefer your web framework's built-in output-escaping for inserting data over hand-rolled functions where possible.
Do not rely on a blocklist of 'bad words' (like banning usernames containing 'script' or 'select') as your primary defense; per the source, missing a single entry defeats it.
caveats: The source's example demonstrates this all with a same-tab self-test (alerting your own cookie); a real attack requires the victim to be logged in and to click a link, which is why 'don't click suspicious links' is not sufficient protection.
Note the distinction between escaping for HTML text context versus other contexts; the source only demonstrates HTML escaping.

cards.title: Why Cross-Site Scripting Is Worse Than Clickjacking for Your Store
cards.summary: Understand the attacker's goal — running code in your origin so they act as a logged-in customer — before choosing defenses.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing remediation when you discover a stored or reflected input vulnerability on a customer-facing page like a profile, review, or search results page.
steps: Recognize that the same-origin policy blocks an attacker from framing your site and reaching into the login form to read a password; XSS is the workaround that gets their code into your page.
Trace what an attacker can then do: take any action as the customer (submit requests with the victim's cookies), or read document.cookie and send it to an attacker server to hijack the session.

Treat any page that mixes attacker-controlled text with your code as a potential injection point, whether it is reflected (in a URL parameter) or stored (saved to your database and shown to other users).

Prioritize fixes for stored injection on pages other customers view, since that enables self-propagating worms (the source's MySpace example added the attacker as a friend and copied the payload into victims' profiles, causing exponential growth and an outage).
When reviewing your store, test your own pages with a harmless proof payload (e.g. alerting the current document cookie) so you confirm the vulnerability without attacking anyone else.
caveats: The source stresses that clients cannot be trusted at all; server-side defenses must hold even if a client is a hacked browser or script.
Worm-style exponential spread is a described historical case study, not a prediction of outcomes for any specific store.

cards.title: Avoid JSONP for Partner Data; Prefer Headers or Proxy
cards.summary: JSONP lets a cooperating server hand you cross-origin data wrapped in a callback, but it grants that origin execution context on your page — consider safer alternatives.
cards.use_when: Deciding how a storefront should read JSON from a partner or internal API that lives on a different origin, especially when the data varies per logged-in user.
steps: Understand the trick: a script tag bypasses the same-origin policy, and JSONP asks the server to wrap its JSON in a caller-specified function name (callback parameter) so the returned script calls your function with the data.

Recognize the dangers: the server must write extra code to support it, some valid JSON is not valid JavaScript (whitespace issues), and the caller controls the callback name, which opens a reflected-file-download / injection class of bug if not sanitized.
From the consuming site's view, including a script from another origin gives that origin remote execution in your page if their response is ever compromised.

Consider alternatives before adopting JSONP: a serverside proxy on your own domain (which also lets you keep the request authenticated to your own session), or a proper CORS-style header that the other server sends to permit your origin to read the response.
If you must relax the boundary intentionally, restrict it narrowly rather than granting full script execution.
caveats: The source describes JSONP as a 'clever hack' that works but is a bad idea for untrusted or unstable partners.
A serverside proxy changes where the request originates and won't reflect per-user logged-in responses the way a browser-side call would.

cards.title: Stop Destructive Request Forgery with SameSite Cookies
cards.summary: SameSite cookies strip the session cookie from cross-site requests so a forged action arrives logged-out and harmless, without blocking the request itself.
cards.use_when: Configuring session cookie attributes for a storefront so cross-site pages can't trigger authenticated actions like account changes or a placed order against a logged-in customer.
steps: Set the SameSite attribute on your session cookies so they are not attached to requests originating from another site.
Use this as your middle-ground control when you want legitimate cross-site form traffic to still reach your server but without acting as the logged-in user.
Combine it with an Origin-header allow list for state-changing POST endpoints, since SameSite alone leaves the request itself arriving (just unauthenticated).
Remember the same mechanism that strips cookies in frames can make an embedded authenticated avatar resolve to the logged-out image on a third-party page.
caveats: SameSite does not prevent the request; it prevents the request from carrying credentials.
The source's lecture describes the mechanism generally; verify the current browser's exact SameSite values and defaults before relying on specific behavior.

cards.title: Treat Script and Image Inclusion as Best-Effort, Not Secure
cards.summary: Blocking hotlinked scripts and images is about bandwidth, not confidentiality, and Referer-based blocking is explicitly unreliable.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how to stop other sites embedding your images, stylesheets or JavaScript (e.g. a signature animation or theme asset they are stealing).
steps: Clarify the goal: for a static image, script or CSS asset, the concern is bandwidth theft (hotlinking), not data leakage, because the asset holds no private data.
Recognize that a hotlinked script runs in the embedding site's page, not yours, so it does not threaten your origin directly.
Use Referer-based checks to reduce casual hotlinking, but accept that the source calls this not foolproof because the header can be manipulated.
For private or per-user assets, prefer unguessable URLs or SameSite-gated responses rather than Referer rules.
Use a CDN (the source cites Google's CDN serving the d3 graphics library) as normal practice for serving such libraries, separate from the hotlinking question.
caveats: The source explicitly lists image/script protection as best-effort; do not treat it as a security boundary.
Origin headers are not sent for simple image/script/style loads, so an Origin allow list won't cover this case.

cards.title: Make Store Input Fields Untrusted by Default
cards.summary: The root condition for both XSS and SQL injection is mixing untrusted customer input with code, so treat every input field as a potential injection vector.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront and back-office features that accept customer text — signup fields, search boxes, review forms, support messages, profile/bio fields — before launch.
steps: For every place customer data is combined with code, name the code context: HTML output, a SQL command, a URL, or JavaScript.
Apply the correct neutralization for that context (HTML escaping for HTML, parameterized queries for SQL) rather than one generic sanitizer.
Prefer frameworks and ORMs that parameterize queries and escape output by default, and confirm they are actually enabled rather than bypassed for convenience.
When the user's data modifies a SQL command, the risk is reading different data or running a second command — the same class of bug as XSS applied to the database.
Include stored fields (bios, reviews, display names) in your review, since stored injection can spread to every visitor's page.
caveats: The source notes the SQL-injection parallel briefly; the detailed lecture focus is XSS.
Blacklisting programmer-sounding usernames is called out as an inadequate defense on its own.

cards.title: Automate Defensive Controls Across All Store Pages
cards.summary: Anti-framing and output-escaping controls should be applied consistently at the site or framework level, not page-by-page where gaps appear.
cards.use_when: Rolling out security headers and escaping after an audit reveals inconsistent coverage across your storefront's templates.
steps: Set frame-ancestors (or the legacy X-Frame-Options header) as a site-wide response header so every page — product, cart, account, admin — refuses untrusted framing.
Enable your web framework's automatic output escaping by default and audit for places where developers disabled or bypassed it.
For each reflected input (URL parameters driving page text), confirm the untrusted value is escaped before it reaches the HTML string.
Add the Origin allow list to your shared POST-handling middleware so new endpoints inherit the check.
Re-test after rollout with self-directed proof payloads on staging to confirm controls fire on every template.
caveats: Retrofitting a site-wide header is easy; retrofitting escaping may require touching many templates and finding old bypasses.
Verify header and attribute support in the browsers your customers actually use before assuming blanket protection.
